According to a 404 Media report, digital forensics company Magnet Forensics says it has found a way to bypass an iPhone security feature that automatically restarts the device if it goes 72 hours without being unlocked. Details below.

['Hacking', ['Background']]

About two years ago, the iOS 18.1 update introduced the "Inactivity Reboot" feature. If an iPhone is not unlocked for 72 consecutive hours, the system will force a restart.

The feature works as follows: after restarting, the device returns to the "Before First Unlock" (BFU) state instead of remaining in the less restricted "After First Unlock" (AFU) state, making it harder for law enforcement and forensic tools to access data on a locked iPhone.

When an iPhone is in the BFU state, some sensitive data remains protected by encryption keys, and these keys only become available after the user enters their passcode for the first time, i.e., once the device enters the AFU state.

After that, more data on the device becomes accessible until the iPhone restarts again, at which point it returns to the BFU state.

The iPhone's automatic restart means that even if law enforcement has seized the device, the phone may already have returned to the BFU state before investigators can access it, because obtaining a search warrant or transporting the device to a forensics lab takes time.

When iOS 18.1 was released, 404 Media noted that this feature also makes it harder for thieves or other bad actors to keep a stolen iPhone in the AFU state in order to research or use intrusion methods.

GrayKey Reportedly Able to Bypass Inactivity Reboot Feature

In a report today, 404 Media said that according to a "tutorial video produced for law enforcement and dated early 2025," Magnet Forensics—the maker of the GrayKey phone unlocking tool—appears to have developed a method to bypass the iPhone's inactivity reboot feature.

The report says Magnet has built a new piece of hardware called GrayKey Preserve, and has also added an "Evidence Preservation Mode" to existing GrayKey hardware.

Both are said to be designed to maintain the iPhone's forensic state, rather than to immediately read the data on the device, allowing law enforcement to keep that state unchanged while awaiting search authorization.

The report noted that while the video does not detail the technical principles of the bypass, it explains that GrayKey can maintain an iPhone's AFU state even after it restarts.

The following is from the report:

404 Media reached out to Apple and Magnet Forensics for comment; neither responded to the request. They also consulted iPhone security researcher Jiska Classen, who said Magnet may have found a way to manipulate the iPhone's clock, or simply shut down the processes responsible for expiring certain data.

Although the video appears to be from early 2025, how long this technology has been available to law enforcement, whether it has been used in actual investigations, and whether it still works against the latest version of iOS all remain unknown.
